final_result.title: Beautiful on the inside: Aesthetic preferences and the skeletal complexity of shapes

findings.consequent: mean normalized skeletal complexity of shapes
findings.mechanism: algorithmic manipulation of shape features
findings.quote: our manipulation of skeletal complexity across levels was successful (F(4,116) = 1174.60, p < 10−5, η² = 0.97)

findings.consequent: probability of being chosen as best painting
findings.mechanism: moderate complexity results in maximal preference (Goldilocks effect)
findings.quote: participants chose moderately complex shapes (54.6%) significantly more frequently than both simple shapes (43.8%; t(192) = 4.97, p = 1.45 × 10-6, d = .36)

findings.consequent: probability of being chosen as best painting
findings.mechanism: moderate complexity results in maximal preference (Goldilocks effect)
findings.quote: and overly complex shapes (42.5%; t(192) = 4.09, p = 6.32 × 10-5, d = .29)

findings.mechanism: inverted-U-shaped relationship between complexity and aesthetic judgments
findings.quote: a significant quadratic term for the relationship between complexity level and chosen probability (b = -1.75, 95%CI[−2.21, -1.29], t = −7.47, p < 2.59 × 10-12)

findings.mechanism: overall effect of complexity on aesthetic preference
findings.quote: a one-way repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant effect of complexity level (F(4,768) = 10.12, p = 1.68 × 10-4, η² = 0.054)

findings.mechanism: L1 is less preferred than L2, L3, L4 as part of the inverted-U relationship
L3 is more preferred than L5 as part of the inverted-U relationship
L4 is more preferred than L5 as part of the inverted-U relationship

findings.consequent: distribution of aesthetic preferences for complexity
findings.mechanism: strong majority of participants preferred moderately complex objects, ruling out bimodal distribution
findings.quote: Among 193 participants, only 34 people were most frequent in choosing simplest objects, and 61 preferred the most complex objects; a strong majority of participants preferred moderately complex objects.

findings.consequent: strength of preference for moderately complex stimuli (vs. simple/overly complex)
findings.mechanism: higher-level notions of complexity (skeletal structure) play a role over-and-above lower-level correlates
findings.quote: moderately complex stimuli were chosen much more often in the Intact group than in the Scrambled group, (with the difference in moderate vs non-moderate being 11.4% for the Intact group vs. 2.9% for the Scrambled group, t(498) = 5.18, p = 3.24 × 10−7, d = .46).

findings.mechanism: overall effect of complexity on aesthetic preference across both groups
findings.quote: a main effect of complexity level (F(3, 1992) = 12.98, p = 1.75 × 10−5, η² = 0.025)

findings.antecedent: interaction between stimulus type (Intact vs. Scrambled) and complexity level
findings.mechanism: beauty relates to complexity differently depending on whether skeletal structure is preserved
findings.quote: a significant interaction between group and complexity (F(4, 1992) = 5.03, p = 0.011, η² = 0.01)

findings.antecedent: skeletal complexity level (quadratic term) in Intact group
findings.mechanism: robust inverted-U relationship between beauty and complexity when skeletal structure is preserved
findings.quote: a robust relationship between beauty and complexity in the Intact group (F(2,248) = 33.12 , p = 1.78 × 10-13), with a significant quadratic term for complexity (b = −1.97, 95%CI[-2.45, -1.49], t = -8.05, p = 3.07 × 10-14)

findings.antecedent: complexity level (quadratic term) in Scrambled group
findings.mechanism: attenuated inverted-U relationship when skeletal structure is destroyed, but lower-level features still contribute to a subtle Goldilocks effect
findings.quote: subtle but significant Goldilocks effect in those who viewed scrambled objects, but this effect was significantly attenuated (mixed-effects model: F(2,248) = 7.42, p = 7.40 × 10–4; quadratic term: b = -0.53, 95%CI[-0.84, -0.22], t = -3.32, p = 0.001).

stimuli.description: Algorithmically generated 2D polygons, manipulated in skeletal complexity (5 levels from simple to complex), stylized as brush drawings, mounted on framed canvases in a virtual room. In Experiment 2, some shapes were 'box-scrambled' by randomizing 6x6 image patches.

limitations: The stimuli were mounted on a fixed background (a gallery room), which might influence participants' choices. Future work could vary the context to see if different environments alter the relationship between complexity and beauty.

tables.description: Summary of daylighting findings for Capistrano district, showing difference in average test improvement (normalized RIT points), statistical certainty, and percentage effect on reading and math scores.
Summary of daylighting findings for Seattle district, showing difference in average test scores (NCE percentage points), statistical certainty, and percentage effect on reading and math scores.
Summary of daylighting findings for Fort Collins district, showing difference in average test scores (normalized RIT points), statistical certainty, and percentage effect on reading and math scores.

limitations: This type of statistical study cannot prove the “cause” for an effect; it merely shows the magnitude of an effect and the certainty of an association between variables.
Less detailed analysis for Seattle and Fort Collins districts, increasing probability of unaccounted factors invalidating results.
Greatest likelihood of other unknown variables influencing findings in Fort Collins district due to limited information on student/school characteristics.
Limited range of window conditions in Fort Collins model may lead to unreported effects of minimum to maximum window area.
Skylights in Fort Collins were often closed by teachers due to poor lighting quality, potentially reducing observed effects.
Study on behavior may be limited by not accounting for daylight exposure outside of the classroom.
